one_liner: Design paper: Oracle Database swaps libaio for io_uring on batched async paths; 29% less CPU per write, sync reads unchanged.
what_it_does: A first-party Oracle paper on replacing libaio with io_uring inside the storage layer of Oracle Database 26ai. There is no library to adopt. io_uring handles the asynchronous paths (DBWR buffer flushes, parallel-query direct-path reads, multi-block reads, redo writes), synchronous single-block reads stay on pread, and each process falls back to libaio on its own if setup fails or a systemic error occurs. The Oracle code is a thin in-house layer over the raw io_uring syscalls (setup/prepare/submit/reap, no liburing). The only public code is a C microbenchmark artifact that exercises read paths.
how_it_is_fast: Syscall amortization: one io_uring_enter submits a batch of 32-4096 I/Os, and completions are reaped by peeking the shared completion queue in user space, where libaio needs io_submit plus io_getevents. Registered (pre-pinned) buffers remove the per-I/O get_user_pages cost, and Table 7 credits them with almost all of the CPU saving (3.66 to 2.58 us per I/O, -29.5%); ring-fd and file-fd registration add only about 1.4%. Each process owns a private ring with IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER and io-wq capped at one worker, because a mutex-shared ring collapsed to 23K IOPS at 128 threads. IOPOLL and SQPOLL were rejected: IOPOLL cost 385 us of CPU per I/O at 128 threads, and SQPOLL threads sit outside the database's cgroup CPU accounting.
when_to_use: You maintain a multi-process or multi-threaded storage engine on Linux NVMe whose background writers or scan workers already submit deep libaio batches (32+ I/Os) and poll for completions. That is the path where the paper measured -29% CPU per write and -19% CPU per scan read.

Your write-flush path is CPU-bound per process. In the DBWR-isolated test, write IOPS rose from 1.07M to 1.43M, and 23 io_uring DBWR processes delivered 1.24M write IOPS against 1.07M from 32 libaio ones.
You want to free CPU at the same throughput, not cut latency. TPC-H CPU per query fell 8.5% (geomean), and scan-heavy queries gained most (Q6 -14.6%, Q1 -12.7%).
You are deciding which I/O paths to port first. Section 3 and Table 7 work as a checklist: batched async paths first, buffer registration before ring-fd or file-fd registration, and no polling modes.
when_not_to_use: Synchronous single-block reads, the most common OLTP I/O. pread and io_uring submit-and-wait matched from 4 KB to 256 KB, and at 512 KB and 1 MB io_uring used about twice the CPU per I/O (16.18 vs 7.33 us, and 27.00 vs 13.44 us) because of io-wq offload.
Small-batch, immediate-reap paths such as redo/WAL writes. With batches of 1-8, libaio and io_uring were indistinguishable (13.32 vs 13.47 us CPU per I/O, same 110 us p99).
When the goal is lower latency or more OLTP throughput. TPC-C tpmC was unchanged, TPC-H elapsed times were within noise, and direct-path read latency was 9.8 vs 9.9 ms.
When you need reusable or reproducible code. The Oracle layer is proprietary, and the Update IOPS, Scan, TPC-C and TPC-H results cannot be rerun outside Oracle.

When you need to share buffers across separate processes on current kernels. Mainline IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS returns -EINVAL when the two rings were created under different mm (Linux 6.14, commit 19d340a, tagged for stable). Since September 2025 it also returns -EEXIST when the source ring is SINGLE_ISSUER and owned by another task. The paper does not explain how its separate Oracle processes get past these checks; threads within one process are not affected.

integration.form: not applicable: design guidance inside closed-source Oracle Database; the public artifact is a source-drop of three standalone C microbenchmarks built with make
integration.dependencies: Oracle layer: raw io_uring syscalls (no liburing), with libaio as the fallback. Artifact: libaio, pthreads, libm, plus Python pandas and matplotlib for the plots
integration.min_toolchain: Artifact: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pthread (compiler version not stated). Kernel: >= 5.11 per the README, >= 6.0 for SINGLE_ISSUER, >= 6.12 for IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS; the exact kernel used for the end-to-end runs is not stated
integration.platforms: Linux only, NVMe with O_DIRECT; end-to-end runs on x86-64 (AMD EPYC 7J13); other architectures not documented
integration.thread_safety: By design, each process or thread owns a private single-issuer ring and shares no ring state. The paper measured a mutex-shared ring as an anti-pattern (22 ms p99 at 128 threads)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — inside Oracle it is a transparent libaio replacement (upper layers cannot tell which interface is in use, and libaio remains the fallback), but nothing reusable ships, so you would reimplement the design in your own engine

gotchas: The artifact's 'shared' registration mode never calls IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS. It issues register opcode 27 (IORING_REGISTER_NAPI in mainline; the code calls it IORING_REGISTER_BUFFERS_SHARE, after the unmerged SHARE_BUF/ATTACH_BUF patches) and ignores the result. So Table 6's shared column (7.5 ms for 200 processes, behind the '270x' claim) measures only ring creation.

Figure 2's libaio baseline runs at depth 1, while the io_uring configurations batch 32-128 I/Os. Its CPU per I/O (CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID) also includes busy-spin think time, which batching spreads over more I/Os. The like-for-like batched libaio vs batched io_uring comparison is Figure 3 (sensitivity_bench, geomean -39%).

Every artifact benchmark is a random read on a raw NVMe device. The write path behind the headline +34% write IOPS, the sync pread comparison (Table 3) and the redo test (Table 8) have no public code.

io_uring_bench.c and sensitivity_bench.c include <linux/io_uring.h> and then redeclare IORING_REGISTER_IOWQ_MAX_WORKERS, IORING_REGISTER_RING_FDS and struct io_uring_rsrc_update. Newer uapi headers already define these, so expect a compile error and a small patch before running (not built here).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: All the siblings (Condy, uring_exec, Asio's io_uring backend, monoio, PhotonLibOS, Seastar) are reusable event loops benchmarked on network servers or echo/ping-pong, and none reports database write-flush or scan numbers. Read this paper when deciding which storage paths in a multi-process engine should move from libaio to io_uring; for code, use liburing or a sibling library, and for a reproducible database study use Jasny et al. (github.com/mjasny/vldb26-iouring), which the paper cites.
verified_claims_summary: The end-to-end runs used an OCI bare-metal AMD EPYC 7J13 (96 vCPUs given to the database, 8 NVMe SSDs in RAID-0, Oracle Linux UEK R8), an internal Oracle Database 26ai build and a libaio baseline, each reported as the vendor's unaudited mean of 3 runs. Switching to io_uring raised DBWR-isolated write IOPS from 1.07M to 1.43M with 29% less CPU per write, cut CPU per direct-path read by 19% at equal throughput and TPC-H CPU per query by 8.5% (geomean), and left TPC-C tpmC unchanged. The database's compiler and flags are not stated; the separate single-NVMe microbenchmarks (gcc -O2, CPU not stated) show -39% CPU per I/O for batched io_uring against batched libaio, as a geomean over 24 block-size x device-count cells.
status_note: The work is active (arXiv v1 in September 2026, artifact v1.1 on Zenodo in May 2026, 'submitted to PVLDB') but is reference-only: the Oracle implementation is closed, and the 1-star artifact repo has no LICENSE file, while Zenodo lists CC-BY-4.0 and the README says it is 'provided for academic evaluation'.
